section: England: key stage 3 (Years 7 to 9), for the statements the Third and Fourth level lessons don't cover

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: Algebraic notation and expanding double brackets (Years 7 to 9)
lessons.intention: We are learning to read and write algebra the short way, and to multiply out two brackets.
criteria: I can write ab for a × b, 3y for y + y + y and 3 × y, and a/b for a ÷ b.
I can write coefficients as fractions rather than decimals, such as ½x rather than 0.5x.
I can expand the product of two binomials, such as (x + 3)(x + 5), and simplify the result.
I can show an expansion as the area of a rectangle, linking the algebra to the picture.

steps.start: Which of these mean the same: 3 × y, y + y + y, y³, 3y, y × 3? Sort them into two groups.
steps.teach: Agree the short forms: ab means a × b, 3y means 3 × y (number first), a² means a × a, and a ÷ b is written as a fraction a/b. A coefficient is written as a fraction, so ½x, not 0.5x. Then draw a rectangle (x + 3) wide and (x + 5) tall, split into four parts: x², 5x, 3x and 15. Add the parts: (x + 3)(x + 5) = x² + 8x + 15. Do (x + 4)(x − 2) with a grid, taking care with the negative: x² − 2x + 4x − 8 = x² + 2x − 8. Point out the pattern: the two numbers add to give the x term and multiply to give the number.
steps.check: Ask them to write m × n ÷ 4 the short way, and to expand (x + 6)(x + 1) and (x − 3)(x + 7).

lessons.home: Find the area of a rectangular room or garden with measurements like (x + 2) metres, by drawing it split into parts.
lessons.vocab: term, coefficient, expression, expand, bracket, binomial, simplify
lessons.understand: Why is (x + 3)² not the same as x² + 9?
lessons.lookFor: Draws or describes the square split into four parts, showing the two 3x pieces that x² + 9 leaves out, so (x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: Using graphs to estimate and solve, and geometric sequences (Years 7 to 9)
lessons.intention: We are learning to read values and solutions from graphs, and to recognise sequences that multiply each time.
criteria: I can read y for a given x, and x for a given y, from a straight-line or curved graph.
I can estimate the solution of two simultaneous linear equations from where their lines cross.
I can use a real-life graph, such as a taxi fare, a cooling drink or a growing population, to estimate an answer.
I can recognise a geometric sequence, find its multiplier and continue it, and spot other sequences such as square and Fibonacci-type numbers.

steps.start: 1, 2, 4, 8, … and 2, 4, 6, 8, … What comes next in each? How are they different?
steps.teach: Show the graph of y = x² and read across and down: when x = 2.5, y is about 6.2; when y = 5, x is about 2.2 (or −2.2). Draw y = x + 1 and y = 5 − x on the same axes: they cross at (2, 3), so x = 2, y = 3 solves both. Read a taxi fare graph that is flat then steep (piece-wise), and a cooling-cup curve that falls fast then slowly, and use them to answer 'how much?' and 'when?' questions, saying it's an estimate. Then compare sequences: in 3, 6, 12, 24 you multiply by 2 each time (geometric); in 3, 6, 9, 12 you add 3 (arithmetic). Find the multiplier by dividing a term by the one before. Mention square numbers and 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 as other sequences.
steps.practise: The "Read it from the graph" sheet.
steps.check: Ask for the next two terms of 2, 6, 18, … and 80, 40, 20, …, and where y = 2x and y = 6 − x cross on a sketch.

lessons.home: Find a graph in the news or on a phone bill, and use it to estimate one value that isn't printed.
lessons.vocab: estimate, intersection, simultaneous, piece-wise, geometric, arithmetic, multiplier, term
lessons.understand: Why is an answer read from a graph an estimate rather than exact?
lessons.lookFor: Explains that you can only read the scale to the nearest small square, and the line or curve has thickness, so the answer is close but may be slightly out.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: One quantity as a fraction of another, and ratios as fractions (Years 7 to 9)
lessons.intention: We are learning to write one amount as a fraction of another, and to see a ratio as fractions and as a straight-line graph.
criteria: I can write one quantity as a fraction of another, less than 1 or greater than 1, using the same units.
I can turn a ratio into fractions of the whole, so in 2 : 3 the first part is ⅖ of the total.
I can say how many times bigger one part of a ratio is than the other, as a fraction.
I can show a ratio as a straight-line graph through (0, 0), such as y = 3/2 x for the ratio 2 : 3.

steps.start: Mia is 120 cm tall and her dad is 180 cm. What fraction of her dad's height is Mia? What fraction of Mia's height is her dad?
steps.teach: Write 'this out of that' as a fraction and simplify: 120/180 = ⅔, and 180/120 = 3/2, which is greater than 1, so it's 1½ times. Units must match first: 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours is 45/120 = 3/8. Then link to ratio: orange and lemon in the ratio 2 : 3 means 5 parts, so orange is ⅖ of the drink and lemon is ⅗; there is ⅔ as much orange as lemon, and 3/2 as much lemon as orange. Make a table of orange and lemon for 2 : 3 (2 and 3, 4 and 6, 6 and 9) and plot it: the points make a straight line through (0, 0), and lemon = 3/2 × orange.
steps.check: Ask for 40p as a fraction of £1, 15 kg as a fraction of 10 kg, and what fraction of the class are girls if boys : girls is 4 : 5.

lessons.home: Mix a drink or a recipe in a ratio, and say what fraction of the whole each ingredient is.
lessons.vocab: fraction, quantity, ratio, part, whole, proportion, improper fraction
lessons.understand: In the ratio 2 : 3, why is the first part ⅖ of the whole and not ⅔?
lessons.lookFor: Explains that ⅔ compares the two parts with each other, but there are 2 + 3 = 5 parts in total, so as a fraction of the whole it is 2 out of 5.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: Sets of numbers and Venn diagrams (Years 7 to 9)
lessons.intention: We are learning to sort things into sets systematically, using tables, grids and Venn diagrams, and to find probabilities from them.
criteria: I can list all the outcomes systematically, using a list, a table or a grid.
I can sort items into a Venn diagram with two sets, including the overlap (intersection) and the region outside both.
I can read a union (A or B or both) and an intersection (A and B) from a Venn diagram, and use them to find a probability.
I can explain that the integers, and the fractions between any two numbers, go on for ever.

steps.start: Name a number that is even and bigger than 10. Now one that is even but not bigger than 10. Now one that is neither.
steps.teach: Draw a rectangle for all the numbers 1 to 15, with two overlapping circles: A = even numbers, B = multiples of 3. Place each number, starting with the overlap (6 and 12). Read off A ∩ B (in both), A ∪ B (in either or both) and the numbers outside both circles. Turn counts into probabilities: if a number from 1 to 15 is picked at random, P(A ∩ B) = 2/15. Fill a Venn diagram from survey numbers by starting with the overlap and taking it away. Show a sample-space grid for two dice as another systematic way to list outcomes. Finish by asking: how many whole numbers are there? How many fractions between 0 and 1? Halve the gap again and again to show there is no end.
steps.practise: The "Sort it in a Venn" sheet.
steps.check: Give a Venn diagram of pupils who play football and tennis. Ask how many play both, how many play only tennis, and P(plays football or tennis).

lessons.home: Ask family members which of two things they like (such as tea and coffee) and draw a Venn diagram of the answers.
lessons.vocab: set, element, Venn diagram, intersection, union, outcome, sample space, infinite
lessons.understand: In a Venn diagram, why do you fill in the overlap first?
lessons.lookFor: Explains that the totals for each set include the overlap, so you need to know the overlap before you can work out how many are only in one set.
